summary: Pupils (age 10–11) learn to name and identify the radius, diameter and circumference of a circle by their DEFINING PROPERTIES — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a straight line from edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across), and the circumference is the distance all the way around — and to apply d = 2r in both directions. The core work is drawing and measuring many circles, tabulating radius against diameter so the invariant d = 2r is discovered rather than told, and practising conversion both ways to guard against the pervasive radius/diameter swap. Several complementary media (dynamic manipulation, paper-and-string measurement, a labelled reference, and a short conversion check) each support a different part of this objective.
misconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.

activities.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
steps: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
activities.insight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.

activities.title: Which line is longest? Predict then measure
steps: On a circle with the centre marked, draw several straight lines from edge to edge — some passing through the centre and some not.
Before measuring, PREDICT which line is the longest and write down why you think so.
Measure each line and compare with your prediction.
Decide which lines pass through the centre (diameters) and which do not (other chords), and explain the difference using the word 'centre'.
activities.insight: The longest straight line across a circle is always the one through the centre — the diameter — so a line that misses the centre is a shorter chord, not a diameter. The pre-stated reason is what reveals a pupil's thinking.

activities.title: Convert both ways and reason aloud
steps: Given a radius (e.g. 4.5 cm), work out the diameter and state how you did it.
Given a diameter (e.g. 10 cm), work out the radius and state how you did it.
For each, say in words whether you doubled or halved and why.
Use a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and use the correct term in each explanation.
activities.insight: Converting diameter-from-radius and radius-from-diameter are different directions of the same relationship; knowing which to double and which to halve, with a reason, prevents the half/twice swap.

activities.title: Feel the circumference as a length
steps: Wrap a length of string once around the edge of a circle, mark where it meets, then straighten it against a ruler to measure the distance around.
Run a finger all the way around the edge and say in your own words what the circumference is.
Contrast this with a straight line drawn across the circle and explain why the circumference is not a straight line.
activities.insight: The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge — a curved length — not a straight line across the circle.

activities.title: Dynamic circle: watch d = 2r hold as the circle resizes (optional screen scaffold)
steps: Drag a point to make the circle bigger and smaller and watch a live readout of the radius and the diameter.
Notice whether the diameter readout always shows twice the radius as the size changes.

Drag the endpoint of a line inside the circle; observe that it is labelled 'diameter — the longest line across' only when it passes through the centre, and is refused the label when it misses the centre.
Say what stays the same (d = 2r) and what must be true for a line to be a diameter (it passes through the centre).
activities.insight: The 2× relationship is invariant across every size, and only a through-centre line earns the name 'diameter' — both the invariant and the defining property made visible together.

activities.title: Labelled circle reference (supporting scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled circle showing centre, radius, diameter and circumference.
Reveal or read each term's defining property: radius = centre to edge; diameter = edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across); circumference = the distance all the way round.
Label parts yourself on circles drawn in varied positions and orientations, including ones where the diameter is slanted.
Match each term to its definition.
activities.insight: Each circle part is identified by its defining property and position relative to the centre, not by a fixed picture orientation.

checkQuestion: A circle has a radius of 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, and how do you know? Then look at this diagram of a circle with its centre marked and three straight lines drawn on it: one from the centre to the edge, one from edge to edge passing through the centre, and one from edge to edge that does NOT pass through the centre. Which line is the radius, which is the diameter, and how can you tell?
checkAnswer: The diameter is 9 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). The centre-to-edge line is the radius and the edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter; a radius goes from the centre to the edge and a diameter passes through the centre, so the third line is neither (it is a chord) because it does not pass through the centre.
